<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1. </span>Implementations</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ Qwen2.5-VL-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as the base video LLM. For efficient training, we adopt LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> with a rank of 128 and an alpha of 256. The learning rate is set to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>. During GRPO training, a batch size of 32 with a group size of 8 is used. The KL constraint coefficient <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is set to 0.005, and the coefficient <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> in the Self-Confirmed Pseudo Reward is set to 0.1. For RL sampling, the temperature, top-p, top-k, and repetition penalty are configured as 1.0, 0.9, 50, and 1.0, respectively, with a maximum turn count <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=3</annotation></semantics></math>.
For coarse-grained video representation during training, we sample <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\mathrm{coarse}}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>coarse</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\mathrm{coarse}}=64</annotation></semantics></math> frames, allocating up to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\mathrm{coarse}}=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>coarse</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\mathrm{coarse}}=16</annotation></semantics></math> tokens per frame. For fine-grained representation, we sample <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\mathrm{fine}}=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>fine</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\mathrm{fine}}=16</annotation></semantics></math> frames with a maximum of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\mathrm{fine}}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>fine</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\mathrm{fine}}=64</annotation></semantics></math> tokens per frame.
During inference, the frame counts remain fixed as above, while the maximum number of tokens per frame is adjusted via input video resolution to align to other baselines on the input length. We evaluate our Video-TwG under two resolution settings: (i) LR (Low Resolution): Matches the training configuration, allowing at most 16 tokens per frame for coarse-grained and 64 tokens per frame for fine-grained representations. (ii) HR (High Resolution): Allows at most 128 tokens per frame for coarse-grained and 512 tokens per frame for fine-grained representations.
In evaluation, temperature is set to 0 and we set a maximum turn count <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=3</annotation></semantics></math> as well. If a prediction cannot be automatically parsed, we revert to the training sampling hyperparameters and retry up to three times. For a fair comparison, both our base model Qwen2.5-VL-7B and other evaluated models that support reasoning are assessed in reasoning mode.
Our training and evaluation framework is built upon ms-swift <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and VLMEvalKit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We leverage vLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite> to accelerate the sampling process. Our training can be implemented on 2 H800 80G GPUs with early-stop strategy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2. </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The baselines used in our experiments are categorized into four groups:
(i) General video LLMs, including Video-LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>,
ShareGPT4Video <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024d</a>)</cite>, and VideoChat2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>;
(ii) Long-context video LLMs, such as LongVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>,
Long-LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin Song and Chen Wu and Eden Duthie, 2024</a>)</cite>,
LongLLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, and Video-XL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>;
(iii) Video agentic systems for long video understanding, represented by
VideoAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> and VideoTree <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025e</a>)</cite>; and
(iv) Video reasoning models, including Video-R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>,
VideoChat-R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, and Long-VILA-R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3. </span>Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our method on multiple-choice questions across three mainstream benchmarks for long video understanding:
Video-MME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, LongVideoBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and MLVU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Video-MME consists of 2,700 manually annotated multiple-choice questions derived from 900 videos.
The videos are divided into three groups based on duration: short (0-2 minutes), medium (4-15 minutes), and long (30-60 minutes).
LongVideoBench contains 3,763 human-labeled questions spanning 6,678 videos, with an average duration of 472 seconds.
The videos are categorized into four duration ranges: 8-15 seconds, 15-60 seconds, 180-600 seconds, and 900-3,600 seconds.
We evaluate models on its validation split, which includes 1,337 multiple-choice questions.
MLVU features videos ranging from 3 to 120 minutes, with an average duration of 15 minutes.
It provides both Dev and Test splits, comprising multiple-choice and open-ended questions.
In this work, we focus on the multiple-choice questions in the Dev split, which contains 2,174 questions covering seven distinct question types.
For all benchmarks, subtitles are not used during evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4. </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the performance of Video-TwG and a wide range of baselines on three representative benchmarks for long video understanding.
Overall, Video-TwG achieves consistently strong performance across datasets with diverse video durations, outperforming general video LLMs, long-context video LLMs, as well as recent reasoning and agent-based approaches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Compared with general-purpose video LLMs, Video-TwG yields substantial improvements on all benchmarks.
On Video-MME, Video-TwG (HR) achieves an overall accuracy of 59.7%, significantly outperforming general video LLMs that typically obtain around 40%.
It also attains 50.0% accuracy on long videos, exceeding prior methods by a large margin, indicating that models primarily designed for short or medium-length videos struggle to generalize to long-duration scenarios.
Video-TwG also consistently outperforms long-context models including LongVA, Long-LLaVA, LongLLaVA, and Video-XL.
For example, on Video-MME, Video-TwG (HR) exceeds Video-XL by over 4 points in overall accuracy, suggesting that effective long-range reasoning is crucial beyond simply increasing the input context length.
Recent video reasoning models, such as Video-R1, enhance long video understanding by introducing explicit reasoning mechanisms.
While effective, these methods rely on reasoning under fixed video context which is not enough for very long temporal contexts, since the model is observed to make up facts confidently when the video information is not enough, which is shown in the case study.
In contrast, Video-TwG achieves stronger performance via grounding and zooming in, indicating more effective long-range temporal modeling.
Agent-based systems, including VideoAgent and VideoTree, address long video understanding through explicit planning or hierarchical decomposition.
Despite their improvements over earlier baselines, they depend on complex multi-stage pipelines that are prone to error accumulation and heavy computations, like captioning.
Video-TwG consistently outperforms VideoTree by 11.7, 6.6 and 8.7 points, and VideoAgent by 12.8, 9.2 and 7.8 points on these benchmarks, respectively, while maintaining a simpler inference paradigm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, under both low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) settings, Video-TwG consistently outperforms its backbone Qwen-2.5-VL-7B across all benchmarks.
The improvements are more pronounced in the low-resolution setting, while models trained under low-resolution still generalize effectively to high-resolution inference.
This indicates that the gains primarily stem from the proposed training paradigm, making Video-TwG particularly effective for real-world and resource-constrained scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5. </span>Ablation Study</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further conduct ablation study to explore the contributions of the core components of our Video-TwG method on the Video-MME benchmark. By default, we adopt the low-resolution setup for its friendly computational costs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>. </span><span id="S4.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablation experiments of different variants of the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B on Video-MME.</span></figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<table id="S4.T2.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S4.T2.5.1" class="ltx_tr">

<div id="S4.T2.6" class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:345.0pt;">
<p id="S4.T2.6.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><sup id="S4.T2.6.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.T2.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">1</span></sup><span id="S4.T2.6.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> Base: Qwen2.5-VL-7B.</span></p>
<p id="S4.T2.6.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><sup id="S4.T2.6.2.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.T2.6.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">2</span></sup><span id="S4.T2.6.2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> Base-TwG-CoT: Base is prompted to perform </span><span id="S4.T2.6.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">think-with-grounding</span><span id="S4.T2.6.2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> using the same prompts as Video-TwG.</span></p>
<p id="S4.T2.6.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><sup id="S4.T2.6.3.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.T2.6.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">3</span></sup><span id="S4.T2.6.3.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> Base-Think: Base is trained on the TwG-51K dataset to conduct text-only reasoning without grounding.</span></p>
<p id="S4.T2.6.4" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><sup id="S4.T2.6.4.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.T2.6.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">4</span></sup><span id="S4.T2.6.4.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> Base-MultiGrained: Base receives both coarse- and fine-grained representations of the entire video as input.</span></p>
<p id="S4.T2.6.5" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><sup id="S4.T2.6.5.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.T2.6.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:80%;">5</span></sup><span id="S4.T2.6.5.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> Base-Think-MultiGrained: Base-Think receives both coarse- and fine-grained representations of the entire video as input.</span></p>
</div></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analysis on the <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span> paradigm.</span>
In Tab. <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we show several experiments on the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B model for analysis on the <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span> paradigm itself. These experiments are conducted to answer these questions. <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i) Can the model benefit from think-with-grounding?</span> We directly prompt the base model to conduct <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span> with the same prompts as applied in Video-TwG (Base-TwG-CoT in Tab. <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
We can see that in the short and medium splits, the improvement is trivial but it has a 1.7 performance gain in the long video split, showing that the base model has the potential to conduct <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span> reasoning to improve the performance, especially in long videos. However, there is still a significant gap between Base-TwG-CoT and our Video-TwG, proving the effectiveness of our method to further enhance <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span> ability.
<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii) Can think-with-grounding go beyond traditional text-only reasoning?</span> We train the base model on the same TwG-51K dataset to make the model conduct text-only reasoning without grounding actions with the GRPO algorithm, whose results are shown in "Base-Think" in Tab. <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Although it achieves improvement compared to the base, there is still a significant gap compared to our method. It is 4.5 lower than our method in long videos.
Our method allows the model to dynamically load fine-grained video to context, which improves the model performance, while text-only RL only helps the model to better grasp the clues in the given fixed multimodal input.
<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(iii) Since think-with-grounding dynamically visits more video input, can such paradigm go beyond directly scaling the video input length?</span> In the Video-MME benchmark, our Video-TwG is observed to conduct 0.65 grounding actions on average per sample. To answer this question, we increase the video input length for the base model, as shown in Base-MultiGrained and Base-Think-MultiGrained in Tab. <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, and we feed the Base and Base-Think with both the coarse- and fine-grained representation of the entire video, which is equivalent to conducting 1 grounding action per sample on the video context length. It shows that such vanilla scaling nearly catches up with our Video-TwG in short videos but there is a significant gap of 5.0(Base-MultiGrained) and 2.4(Base-Think-MultiGrained) in long videos, showing the necessity of intelligent selection of video clip, especially in long videos.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analysis on our two-stage curriculum training strategy.</span> We compare our Video-TwG with two variants, when it’s trained with stage 1 or 2 only. The results are shown in Fig. <a href="#acmlabel4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, which shows that the performance drops significantly when either of training stages is skipped. It’s noted that if skipping the stage 1, the model’s grounding action vanishes quickly in the early stage of the training during stage 2, indicating the necessity of stage 1 as a good cold-start, and the the model’s performance in long videos is 1.4 inferior to when it is trained in stage 1. When equipped with stage 1 and stage 2, the model gradually grasp the <span id="S4.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span> ability and achieves the best performance.</p>
</div>

</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analysis around the grounding reward in stage 1 training.</span>
We explore the roles of several core factors in stage 1 training, the accuracy-gated mechanism, the grounding reward <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{grounding}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>grounding</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{grounding}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the soft grounding reward <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{soft}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>soft</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{soft}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the hard grounding reward <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>hard</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{hard}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows the curves of the number of turns and the accuracy reward during the stage 1 training. We can see that without <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{grounding}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>grounding</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{grounding}}</annotation></semantics></math> or without <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>hard</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{hard}}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{grounding}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>grounding</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{grounding}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the grounding action vanishes along with the training process, showing that the signal provided by <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{soft}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>soft</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{soft}}</annotation></semantics></math> is too weak to boost the model to learning <span id="S4.SS5.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span>. Only with <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>hard</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{hard}}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{grounding}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>grounding</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{grounding}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the training is unstable where the model collapses at around 800 steps when the model quickly forgets the grounding action. Compared to <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{soft}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>soft</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{soft}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>hard</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{hard}}</annotation></semantics></math> fails to provide diversified and differentiated rewards in a group, which makes the training process less stable compared to <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{soft}}+R_{\mathrm{hard}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>soft</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>hard</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{soft}}+R_{\mathrm{hard}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Without the accuracy gated mechanism, the model learns slightly quickly to think with grounding, but however, it achieves much lower accuracy rewards than our standard model in stage 1. The grounding and accuracy targets may conflict on some samples, thereby affecting the performance. We conduct quantitative evaluation for model without accuracy-gated mechanism in stage 1, as shown in Tab. <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, which shows it is 0.5 and 1.5 lower than the standard model in the long and overall splits.</p>
</div>

<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18702v1/case_study_v2.png" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/242;" width="476" height="242" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>. </span><span id="S4.F7.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The case study on Video-R1, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Our Video-TwG. The location of the crucial video clues for this question is marked with <span id="S4.F7.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#00E000;">green</span> boxes.</span><span id="acmlabel11" class="ltx_acm_description ltx_centering ltx_nodisplay"></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analysis on the Self-Confirmed Pseudo Reward <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>pseudo</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}</annotation></semantics></math> in stage 2 training.</span>
Fig. <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> illustrates the training dynamics of the number of turns and accuracy reward during stage 2. Both settings exhibit a similar trend: the number of grounding actions first decreases and then increases. This suggests that grounding is not always necessary for all questions, the model learns to answer questions with fewer grounding actions in the early stage of training, leading to a reduction in turns. As training progresses, the model realizes that additional grounding can further improve accuracy, and the number of turns begins to rise. Correspondingly, accuracy rewards start to increase more steadily after the turning points (around 700 steps for "stage 2 w/o <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>pseudo</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}</annotation></semantics></math> " and 900 steps for "stage 2").
With the introduction of the Self-Confirmed Pseudo Reward <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>pseudo</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the model learns to invoke grounding actions more adaptively, using fewer grounding steps on average while achieving higher accuracy rewards throughout training. As shown in Tab. <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, removing <math id="S4.SS5.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>pseudo</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}</annotation></semantics></math> leads to a slight performance drop, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing redundant grounding actions without sacrificing overall performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyze the number of samples containing grounding actions for Video-TwG w/o <math id="S4.SS5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>pseudo</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}</annotation></semantics></math> and Video-TwG in Tab. <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Video-TwG reduces the number of such samples by 15.7%, approximately 300, indicating more selective grounding behavior. To assess the grounding quality, we evaluate QA performance when only the last grounded video clip is provided as input as an approximation to the grounding quality. For objectivity, we employ InternVL-3.5-38B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025c</a>)</cite> as an external evaluator, sampling 32 frames with 256 tokens per frame. Results in Tab. <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> show that grounding clips produced by standard Video-TwG yield better QA performance, with gains of 2.1 and 1.6 on the long and overall splits, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, these results indicate that <math id="S4.SS5.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>pseudo</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\mathrm{pseudo}}</annotation></semantics></math> encourages more effective and cautious grounding strategies, particularly for reducing useless exploration in long videos. The model learns to avoid unnecessary grounding actions that do not contribute to answering the question, leading to both higher efficiency and better grounding quality.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>. </span><span id="S4.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The number of samples that has grounding action on Video-MME benchmark.</span></figcaption>
<table id="S4.T5.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S4.T5.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T5.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.7pt 5.0pt;" rowspan="2"><span id="S4.T5.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Method</span></th>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6. </span>Case Study</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present a qualitative case study comparing the responses of Video-R1, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and our method, which is shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.5. Ablation Study ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ Think with Grounding: Curriculum Reinforced Reasoning with Video Grounding for Long Video Understanding" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.
Given a fixed and sparse video context from a long video, Video-R1 produces substantially longer reasoning traces than Qwen2.5-VL-7B; however, its reasoning process is chaotic and leads to hallucinated conclusions, confidently identifying the tool as orange despite being incorrect.
The base model Qwen2.5-VL-7B recognizes that key visual clues are missing in the initial coarse-grained video input, which ultimately results in an incorrect answer.
In contrast, our method explicitly expresses uncertainty in its initial prediction and performs a grounding action in the first turn.
After receiving fine-grained visual input from the grounded video clip, it successfully identifies the correct answer.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5. </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduce Video-TwG, a curriculum reinforced framework that enables video LLMs to think with grounding in a multi-turn reasoning process, zooming into question-relevant clips only when necessary. To support scalable training, we construct the TwG-51K dataset and propose a two-stage reinforced curriculum strategy that cold-starts on short-video GQA with grounding labels and then scales to the full dataset to improve generalization. Moreover, to handle complicated <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span> reasoning for various kinds of data, we develop a TwG-GRPO algorithm which features the fine-grained grounding reward, self-confirmed pseudo reward, and accuracy-gated mechanism.
Extensive experiments on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU demonstrate consistent advantages over strong baselines. Our results validate the effectiveness of our two-stage reinforced curriculum strategy: training with low-resolution inputs consistently enhances the base model’s <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">think-with-grounding</span> ability across different inference resolutions, while TwG-GRPO better leverages diverse unlabeled data to improve grounding quality and reduce redundant groundings without sacrificing QA performance.
In future work, we plan to go beyond trajectory-level optimization by developing fine-grained process reward modeling and single-step training under more complex constraints, aiming to build more powerful and efficient long video reasoning models.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
